title: How to Get a 7 in IB Economics
summary: Learn how to get a 7 in IB Economics with a realistic study plan covering assessment objectives, command terms, diagrams, essays, data and the IA.
body_markdown:
Getting a 7 in IB Economics requires more than memorizing definitions. You must combine accurate theory with diagrams, real-world application, data interpretation, evaluation, and disciplined exam technique. The most reliable approach is to study according to the **four assessment objectives** , practise each paper in its actual format, and correct recurring weaknesses.


This guide explains what top-level performance looks like at SL and HL. It also provides practical methods for Paper 1, Paper 2, HL Paper 3, and the Internal Assessment portfolio.


### Understand how IB Economics is assessed


The course covers introduction to economics, microeconomics, macroeconomics, and the global economy. According to the official[IB Economics course overview](https://ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/curriculum/individuals-and-societies/economics/) , SL and HL students complete written examinations and a portfolio of three commentaries.


Component SL weighting HL weighting Main demand


Paper 1 30% 20% Extended analysis and evaluation


Paper 2 40% 30% Data-response questions using extracts


Paper 3 Not assessed 30% HL policy analysis and calculations


Internal Assessment 30% 20% Three economic commentaries


Paper 1 lasts **1 hour 15 minutes** , while Paper 2 lasts **1 hour 45 minutes** . HL students also sit Paper 3 for **1 hour 45 minutes** . These details are confirmed in the official[SL Economics subject brief](https://www.ibo.org/globalassets/new-structure/programmes/dp/pdfs/sl-economics-en.pdf) and[HL Economics subject brief](https://www.ibo.org/globalassets/new-structure/programmes/dp/pdfs/hl-economics-en.pdf) .


A grade 7 does not correspond to one permanently fixed percentage. Boundaries can change between examination sessions, so historical boundaries are planning references rather than guaranteed targets. Judge your readiness through several timed assessments and aim comfortably above previous boundaries.


### Master the four assessment objectives


Knowing economics is not enough if your answer does not demonstrate the assessed skill. The IB organizes these skills into four **assessment objectives** , or AOs.


Objective What it requires Strong performance


**AO1** Knowledge and understanding Precise definitions and secure theory


**AO2** Application and analysis Context-specific causal reasoning


**AO3** Synthesis and evaluation Balanced arguments and justified judgments


**AO4** Appropriate skills Accurate diagrams, calculations, and terminology


Revision must test all four objectives. If you can define inflation but cannot analyse a cost-push inflation diagram, apply it to an extract, or evaluate possible policies, the topic is not exam-ready.


### Follow command terms precisely


A **command term** identifies the task required. Treating “explain,” “discuss,” and “evaluate” as interchangeable produces relevant but poorly targeted answers.


Command term group Examples Required response


**AO1** Define, describe, outline, state Provide precise information at the requested depth


**AO2** Analyse, apply, explain, suggest Develop causal links and apply theory


**AO3** Discuss, evaluate, examine, justify Consider competing arguments and reach a judgment


**AO4** Calculate, construct, draw, plot Demonstrate the relevant technical skill


For example, **explain** requires reasons or causes. An answer about an indirect tax should trace how the tax raises firms’ costs, shifts supply left, increases equilibrium price, and reduces quantity.


**Evaluate** requires an appraisal of strengths and limitations. Relevant considerations could include elasticity, stakeholder effects, administrative costs, unintended consequences, and short-run compared with long-run outcomes. Finish by identifying the conditions under which the policy is most likely to succeed.


### Build usable knowledge and diagrams


Passive rereading creates familiarity rather than reliable recall. For every syllabus subtopic, practise five tasks without notes:


1. Define essential terms accurately.
2. Explain the model through a causal chain.
3. Draw and label the relevant diagram.
4. Apply the model to a specific situation.
5. Evaluate assumptions, stakeholders, limitations, and alternatives.


Use[IB Economics Flashcards](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-economics/flashcards) for definitions, formulas, labels, and short analytical sequences. Do not memorize complete evaluation paragraphs because evaluation must respond to the particular context.


Build a bank of approximately **8-12 adaptable real-world examples** across microeconomics, macroeconomics, and the global economy. For each one, record the country, policy or event, a concrete detail, the relevant model, affected stakeholders, and one limitation.


Practise drawing each core diagram from memory in about two minutes. Include axes, curves, equilibria, movement arrows, and relevant welfare areas. In your written analysis, refer explicitly to labels and explain why a curve shifts and what the new equilibrium means. The[RevisionDojo Economics resources hub](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-economics) can help you connect diagrams with topic-based questions.


### Use a repeatable method for each paper


### Paper 1: extended responses


Paper 1 rewards developed reasoning rather than numerous disconnected points. Define central terms, use an appropriate diagram, and construct a complete causal chain. Each paragraph should directly advance the answer.


For evaluation, consider:


- short-run and long-run effects;
- winners and losers;
- elasticity and responsiveness;
- assumptions behind the model;
- costs, time lags, and enforcement;
- efficiency, equity, sustainability, or economic well-being;
- alternative or complementary policies.


A strong conclusion identifies what the outcome depends on and decides which consideration matters most. The[Economics topic-by-topic revision guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-economics-topic-by-topic-revision) can help connect content revision to paper-specific practice.


### Paper 2: data response


Paper 2 tests whether you can apply economics to unfamiliar material. Read the questions, identify command terms and marks, and select the extract evidence relevant to each response.


Do not copy a quotation and assume that it counts as application. Connect a specific detail to theory, a diagram, or an economic consequence. For calculations, show your method, include appropriate units, and interpret the result.


Longer answers should repeatedly return to the case. Evaluation based on the country’s economic conditions, development level, institutions, or policy constraints is stronger than a generic list of advantages and disadvantages.


### Paper 3: HL policy work


HL Paper 3 combines quantitative and qualitative reasoning. Practise required calculations until you can choose the formula, substitute correctly, show working, and interpret the result without prompts.


Policy recommendations must follow from the evidence. Compare realistic options, explain transmission mechanisms, consider trade-offs, and recommend a policy or policy mix with supporting reasons. Use the[IB Economics Questionbank](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-economics/questionbank) to isolate weak topics, then attempt[Economics predicted and mock papers](https://www.revisiondojo.com/predicted-papers) under timed conditions.


### Make evaluation lead to a judgment


Evaluation is not a separate paragraph containing memorized disadvantages. It should test the strength of the analysis by asking which assumptions hold, whose outcomes matter, how effects change over time, and what evidence would alter the conclusion. A useful approach is to identify the factor that most strongly determines whether the proposed outcome occurs.


Suppose a question asks whether higher indirect taxes will reduce consumption of cigarettes. Relevant evaluation includes the price elasticity of demand, the size of the tax, consumer addiction, possible illegal markets, effects on low-income households, government revenue, and the time required for habits to change. These points should not be presented as an unconnected list. Explain how each consideration changes the policy’s effectiveness or desirability.


A strong judgment could conclude that taxation is likely to reduce consumption gradually, but that its effectiveness depends on demand becoming more elastic over time and on enforcement against illegal sales. It might then recommend combining taxation with information campaigns or support for quitting. This is stronger than stating only that the outcome “depends on elasticity” because it weighs the evidence and identifies a realistic policy response.


### Manage examination time deliberately


Before writing, divide available time according to the demands and marks of each question. Reserve planning time for extended responses and checking time for calculations, labels, units, and unanswered parts. A concise plan should identify definitions, the main analytical chain, a diagram, contextual evidence, two or three evaluation angles, and the likely judgment.


If you become stuck, write the economic mechanism in simple steps before turning it into full prose. For example: higher interest rates increase borrowing costs, consumption and investment fall, aggregate demand shifts left, and inflationary pressure may decrease. This prevents missing links and makes the final explanation easier to follow.


Do not spend excessive time perfecting one diagram or introductory paragraph. Marks come from the complete response, so unfinished evaluation or omitted calculations are costly. During timed practice, record where you were at fixed intervals. If you repeatedly fall behind, shorten planning notes, make definitions more concise, and practise producing diagrams without unnecessary detail.


### Treat the Internal Assessment seriously


The IA consists of **three commentaries** , each based on a published news extract from a different syllabus unit, excluding the introductory unit. Each commentary uses a different key concept and has an official limit of **800 words** . The portfolio is assessed by your teacher and externally moderated by the IB.


A strong article gives you a clear economic problem, usable contextual evidence, and a policy or development that can be analysed. Each commentary should:


- introduce the issue and key concept concisely;
- apply theory directly to the article;
- include and explain a relevant diagram;
- evaluate stakeholders, assumptions, time periods, and alternatives;
- finish with a supported judgment.


Complete the portfolio steadily so it does not compete with final exam revision. The[RevisionDojo Economics IA guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ia-guides/ib-economics) explains planning and criteria, but all feedback must be used according to your school’s academic integrity rules.


### Follow an eight-week IB Economics study plan


This plan assumes approximately **6-8 focused hours per week** . If time is limited, reduce the number of questions rather than skipping correction.


Week Main focus Required output


**1** Diagnosis Timed section, syllabus audit, and error log


**2** Microeconomics Retrieval, diagrams, analysis, and evaluation


**3** Macroeconomics AD-AS, policies, examples, and timed writing


**4** Global economy Trade, development, data, and evaluation


**5** Paper 1 Two plans, one timed response, and correction


**6** Paper 2 and HL calculations Timed data response and quantitative drills


**7** Mixed mock Complete paper, marking, and targeted repair


**8** Consolidation Second mock, diagrams, examples, and retrieval


Use two weekly sessions for retrieval and diagrams, two for exam questions, one for timed work, and one for marking. Keep recovery time in the schedule because exhaustion reduces the quality of analysis.


### Turn mistakes into improvement


Completing papers does not automatically produce **IB Economics top marks** . Maintain an error log that classifies each lost mark as knowledge, application, analysis, evaluation, diagram, calculation, or timing.


Correct the specific problem, then attempt a fresh question testing the same skill several days later. For example, repair a weak causal chain by writing every intermediate step, or improve generic evaluation by adding stakeholders, conditions, and a reasoned judgment. Jojo AI can question your reasoning and identify missing links, but the final retest should be completed independently.


Common mistakes include memorizing inflexible essays, using vague examples, failing to explain diagrams, copying data without interpretation, omitting calculation working, and concluding only that “it depends.” Mark work strictly rather than rewarding what you intended to write. The[RevisionDojo Grade Calculator](https://www.revisiondojo.com/grade-calculator) can help interpret practice results, although it provides an estimate rather than an official predicted grade.


### Conclusion


To get a 7 in IB Economics, master the syllabus while training **AO1-AO4** through retrieval, application, timed practice, correction, and delayed retesting. Strong answers combine accurate theory, diagrams, contextual evidence, complete analytical chains, and evaluation ending in a justified judgment.


RevisionDojo can support this process through Economics Study Notes, Flashcards, the Questionbank, Jojo AI, IA guidance, and Mock Exams. Begin with a timed diagnostic, classify every lost mark, and use the most relevant tools to repair your largest weaknesses.
